There was something odd about working for Steiner, Maria Gottlieb had to admit. He was a fair boss. His workers and employees loved him to death. She suspected most of them would take a bullet for him. A part of her wondered what Steiner would be like if he’d decided to start a cult rather than try to become Chancellor of Germany. He’d certainly make more money. Although, she had to admit ,the finances she was allowed to work with there nothing short of impressive. People gave heartily to the DNVP. And there was something here about a profitable enterprise being run down in Liberia, too.

It was certainly more than what she’d had to work with the AfD.

As head of DNVP’s propaganda department, for lack of a more appropriate term, she had a hefty burden on her shoulder. Yet people deferred to her. Respected her. It as almost as if she were their queen rather than their boss.

Despite the chill outside, which frosted on her office’s windows, the inside of the DNVP’s Saxony office was just right. Not too hot, not too cold. It didn’t hurt that her room had a personal thermostat, though a part of her did suspect it was just for show.

Her chair was nice, her desk was good. She had a(n empty) bookshelf. And Steiner had given her a potted plant named Hans. No, she didn’t know why it was named Hans. Steiner had simply given her the houseplant and declared it Hans. and that she’d have to walk it, feed, love it, and somesuch.

She had one of her interns do that for her.

Mari’s actual job consisted of making plots, planning media and marketing campaign, and the like. She’d helped organize this year’s Day of German Unity, and given it the genius idea to be not just marches but community works. It’s attracted so many people. Everything was a success. She was even planning to advertise for Steiner’s next warpath series of speeches.

With everything Steiner afforded her, she had trouble hating him.

Maria blinked. Why was Steiner always on her mind?

Someone knocked on her door. She kept it open to create an air of approachability. Which was admittedly hard when Steiner made sure she always had a pair of burly Stahlhelms guarded her at all times. They were not a very talkative due to, either.

When she looked up to see who was there, she saw Steiner standing here. He was leaning his back against the doorframe, holding a red box. As she looked at it, she saw it to be in the shape of a heart.

“What?” she managed, unsure of what to say.

Steiner turned to face her direct. Clad in a blue blazer, that smile of his made it downright impossible to dislike him. Holding the heart-shaped box, he strode towards her desk. “I hope you don’t mind me barging in on you like this.”

“A little. I was getting the final touches ready of advertising the series of speeches you want to make. A hard month’s worth, y’know?”

The man cocked a brow. “Care to take a break?”

“Do I have to?” she asked with a little smile. Maria felt so small before Steiner. It reminded her of how she’d held when they’d first met.

Her family had been driving and had gotten horribly lost. It had been such a good day; Maria had just gotten a brand new doll. But then they had been assailed by a gang of thug who forced out of their car. Just as they were being robbed and little Maria had started to bawl her eyes, some tall big kid and what she presumed was his younger brother stepped out of the shadows.

Next thing she knew, the thugs were either on the ground crying out or were running away with limps. The big kid’s younger brother, who was actually Erik Falkenrath, helped return the robbed money to Maria’s parents. The big kid had picked up her doll, handed it to her, and tussled her blonde hair. “Everything’s all right,” he had said. “I won’t let anyone hurt you.”

And just like that she had stopped crying.

That was then. And this was now.

Steiner shook his head. “You don’t have to. But then you’ll never find out what’s in the box.”

Maria bit the inside of her lip. “Okay, shoot. What’s inside, boss?”

His cocked his hand and gave her an over-the-top sad look. Steiner had missed his calling, Maria thought. He’d’ve made for a great actor. And a cult leader. An actor who led a cult? “C’mon, Maria. We know our names. Use ’em.”

“Fine. What’s in the box, Steiner?” Maria said. Ever since she’d first met him, she’d just called him ‘Steiner’. He insisted everyone call him that. Although she was sure she’d learned his name earlier from Erik, even used it once or twice, he’d first actually told his first name to her after they’d slept together all those years ago. She’d been a blossoming young woman then, and he a hardy veteran fresh from the service.

Steiner handed her the box. “Open it up. See for yourself.”

Maria rolled her eyes and did so. It was full of chocolates. A mangeria of choices, every kind of chocolate she could imagine, It’s looked expensive. This was a lot ,and it was from a pricy company. “I… what?” she tried.

“It’s the 14th,” Steiner said with a shrug.

“Huh?” she asked, at a loss for words.

“Valentines Day, ya ditz,” he said with a smile. “It’s not so German, but I found it a nice holiday regardless.” The man made little heart with his fingers over his breast. “Be my Valentine?”

Maria could only stare at the man. She felt a heat in her breast that spread to her cheeks. “I… no way!” It sounded so weak.

Steiner gave her a childish frown. “Pretty please with sugar on top? I’ll buy you dinner. Name a restaraunt. I don’t care if the place is reserved six months in advance. I’ll get us a table tonight.”

“Screw you,” she said, but she couldn’t help but smiling. Her own body was betraying her!

“So, pick you up at seven, leave work, and get food then?” He winked.

Her treacherous flesh actually made her nod to that. Her throat was too dry to protest. In some dark pit of her heart, she just really liked the idea of dinner with Steiner.
